## Synthesis: A Proposed Method for Locating and Quantifying a Sputtered Gold Layer via Spectral X-ray Transmission

### Objective and Approach
The goal of this analysis is to propose and evaluate the feasibility of a method to map the spatial distribution of a sputtered gold (Au) layer and estimate its thickness using the characteristic Au K-edge absorption jump at approximately 80.7–80.8 keV. In a transmission X-ray measurement, gold reveals itself not through emission peaks but through a sudden increase in absorption above its K-edge energy: photons just above the edge are strongly attenuated where gold is present, while photons just below pass through relatively unimpeded. By comparing transmitted intensity above and below this edge, one could in principle locate the gold and, through the Beer-Lambert attenuation law, infer its areal thickness. Note that the empirical results below (a detected, coherent gold layer and its quantified thickness) have not been verified here, because no spatial maps, component images, or validation plots were available for inspection; the treatment is therefore framed as method proposal and expected behavior rather than confirmed findings.

### The Reference Illumination Spectrum
The companion baseline (I0) dataset provides the incident X-ray spectrum measured without the gold-attenuating effect of interest, and it is essential context for interpreting the transmission data. Its spatial-mean spectrum shows the expected shape of a 160 kVp bremsstrahlung source: a broad continuum that rises from low energies, peaks in the intermediate energy range, and tails off toward the maximum accelerating voltage. Superimposed on the continuum are several sharp lines that correspond to characteristic fluorescence/target lines and detector response features. The continuum retains photon flux extending toward the ~80.8 keV region; however, whether the counts in the above-edge window are sufficient for a low-noise edge-jump measurement has not been quantified here (e.g., counts/pixel and SNR in the above-edge window remain to be established) and should not be assumed adequate. Because the bremsstrahlung continuum is inherently weaker above ~80.8 keV, this above-edge flux is the crux of the measurement and must be assessed quantitatively before quantification. This baseline should be used as a per-pixel normalization (dividing the measured cube by I0) so that variations in illumination and detector efficiency are removed and the residual signal reflects true sample attenuation.

### Interpreting the Gold Signature
Because gold in transmission is defined by an absorption edge rather than a distinct emission phase, the most robust way to quantify it would be a physically-motivated edge-jump calculation rather than a purely statistical decomposition. The recommended metric is the ratio (or log-ratio) of normalized transmitted intensity in a narrow energy window just below the edge to that just above the edge. Where gold is present, transmission drops sharply above the edge (attenuation increases), producing a large edge-jump value; where gold is absent, the transmission changes smoothly across this energy and the edge-jump value stays near zero. As a hard prerequisite before any quantification, one must verify that none of the characteristic fluorescence/target lines or detector response features identified in the baseline spectrum falls within the narrow below-edge or above-edge windows around 80.8 keV, since a line landing in either window would corrupt the intensity ratio. Converting the edge-jump magnitude into thickness would use the known mass-attenuation coefficients of gold on either side of the K-edge together with its bulk density. In the ideal single-energy Beer-Lambert limit, the logarithm of the below/above intensity ratio scales linearly with the areal amount of gold along the beam path; with finite energy windows, beam hardening, and a polychromatic source, this linearity is only approximate and holds best for thin films analyzed with narrow, near-monochromatic windows.

### Expected Spatial Architecture (Anticipated, Not Yet Observed)
The following describes what a sputtered gold layer would be expected to produce, not what has been observed in this dataset. A sputtered layer typically produces a spatially coherent gold-bearing region — often a patch or deposited film footprint — with graded edges reflecting the sputter deposition profile (thicker in the center of the deposition zone, thinning toward the margins). A well-behaved analysis would therefore be expected to show a structured, contiguous high-signal region in the edge-jump map rather than scattered isolated pixels, and the distribution of edge-jump values across the field would be expected to show a population of gold-bearing pixels separated from a background population. However, no edge-jump map, value-distribution histogram, or spatial map was available for verification, so it CANNOT be confirmed here that (a) a spatially coherent, contiguous gold-bearing region exists, (b) the value distribution is bimodal/separated, or (c) the signal is distinguishable from salt-and-pepper noise. Such a structured spatial pattern combined with a physically reasonable value distribution would, if observed, indicate a real feature rather than noise — but this must be demonstrated, not assumed.

### Confidence Assessment and Caveats
The strength of this approach is that it is anchored to a known, element-specific physical transition (the Au K-edge at ~80.7–80.8 keV) and to a measured illumination reference. This means the method is *capable* of high-confidence localization IF a coherent spatial structure is actually observed in the edge-jump map. It is important to stress that this is a methodological argument about the physical anchoring of the technique, not evidence that gold has been detected in this dataset: no actual edge-jump map result is presented here, so a high-confidence localization claim for this specific sample cannot yet be supported. Thickness estimates would carry more uncertainty and should be treated as semi-quantitative: at 0.250 mm spatial resolution and 0.1 keV energy binning the edge would in principle be finely sampled in energy, but this presumes the dataset actually extends to and adequately samples the ~81 keV region with sufficient counts — which has not been confirmed. Accuracy would further depend on (1) clean normalization by the I0 baseline, (2) adequate photon counts above 80.8 keV where the source continuum is weaker, (3) verification that no characteristic/artifact line falls within the edge windows, and (4) the assumption of uniform gold density in the sputtered film. Regions with very thin gold or low above-edge flux would have noisier thickness estimates. Any apparent gold signal that does not form a spatially coherent structure, or that coincides with detector artifact lines seen in the baseline spectrum, must be rejected rather than reported as real gold.

### Unified Physical Model
Taken together, the physical framework supports a candidate model in which the sample would consist of a spatially defined sputtered gold deposit sitting on a low-attenuation substrate, imaged against a bremsstrahlung continuum that must provide sufficient above-edge flux for quantification. In this proposed model, gold would be localized by the presence of a sharp transmission decrease across ~80.8 keV, and its thickness mapped by the magnitude of that edge jump interpreted through the Beer-Lambert law. This framework addresses the stated objective at the level of method design: it describes how gold location could be determined from the element-specific K-edge, and how thickness could be recovered as a semi-quantitative map modulated by counting statistics in the high-energy tail of the source. The empirical confirmation of a detected gold layer and a quantified thickness map remains to be demonstrated with the actual spatial maps and validation plots.

### Key Evidence
- **baseline_I0 (spatial-mean spectrum)**: Shows the incident 160 kVp bremsstrahlung continuum and its characteristic/detector lines, and provides the per-pixel normalization reference needed to isolate true sample attenuation from source and detector variations. It indicates photon flux extending toward the Au K-edge region (~80.8 keV), but the adequacy of above-edge counts for a low-noise edge-jump measurement has not been quantified here and remains the key open question for feasibility.

scientific_claims.claim: A sputtered gold layer could in principle be spatially localized in transmission spectral X-ray imaging by detecting the sharp increase in attenuation across the gold K-edge at approximately 80.7–80.8 keV; this is a proposed, physically-anchored method, and localization in this specific dataset has not been empirically verified here.
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: If validated on real spatial maps, establishing that element-specific K-edge contrast reliably locates thin sputtered metal films would support high-energy spectral X-ray imaging as a non-destructive tool for mapping metallic coatings, with applications in materials quality control and thin-film metrology.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone used the gold K-edge absorption jump near 80 keV in transmission spectral X-ray imaging to spatially map a sputtered gold layer?

scientific_claims.claim: The areal thickness of a thin sputtered gold film could be estimated from the magnitude of the K-edge transmission jump using the Beer-Lambert law with known mass-attenuation coefficients, with the caveat that the underlying log-ratio-to-thickness linearity holds only approximately for thin films analyzed with narrow, near-monochromatic windows under a polychromatic source. This thickness recovery has not been demonstrated on the present dataset.
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: If demonstrated, quantitative thickness recovery from a single K-edge jump would provide a self-calibrating, element-specific approach to film thickness metrology that does not require destructive cross-sectioning or separate reference standards.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone quantified thin metal film thickness from the magnitude of a K-edge absorption jump in energy-resolved X-ray transmission data?

dynamic_analysis_records.target: For every pixel, form the transmission spectrum by dividing the primary datacube by the same-grid baseline_I0 operand (gate out low-flux pixels where I0 is near zero), and work in optical depth -ln(I/I0). Measure the Au K-edge step at 80.8 keV using the measure_edge_step helper (let it pick robust pre-/post-edge windows and flag where the edge is measurable). Map the edge-step magnitude to locate the Au (Au_Edge_Step). Then convert the measured optical-depth jump into Au thickness: obtain the Au mass-attenuation coefficients just below and just above the K-edge from the attenuation helper (element 'Au'), take the difference in mu across the edge, and invert delta(optical depth) = delta(mu)*rho*t using bulk Au density to produce a per-pixel thickness map (Au_Thickness) in appropriate length units. Report thickness only where the edge is deemed measurable; set non-Au / low-flux pixels to zero or NaN so the spatial map shows the sputtered Au distribution cleanly.

def analyze_feature(data, axis, auxiliary=None):
    from scilink.skills._shared.edge_step import measure_edge_step
    from scilink.skills._shared.xray_attenuation import attenuation

    # ---- shapes ----
    H, W, E = data.shape
    energy = np.asarray(axis, dtype=float)

    # ---- I0 operand (required for transmission) ----
    if auxiliary and "baseline_I0" in auxiliary:
        i0 = np.asarray(auxiliary["baseline_I0"], dtype=float)
    else:
        # fall back to a spatial-mean flat field so the tool can still run
        i0 = np.broadcast_to(np.nanmean(data.reshape(-1, E), axis=0),
                             data.shape).copy()

    edge_kev = 80.8

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 1: honest per-pixel Au K-edge measurement at 80.8 keV.
    # Use the registered edge-step helper: it forms -ln(I/I0), gates
    # on flux, picks robust wide continuum windows, and reports whether
    # the edge is actually measurable (refuses flux-starved edges).
    # We DO NOT pivot to the L3 edge -- the K-edge is the only
    # Au-specific fingerprint. If it is not measurable, we honestly
    # return zeros rather than fabricating a border/speckle artifact.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    r = measure_edge_step(
        data, i0, energy, edge_kev,
        pre_gap=2.0, post_gap=1.0, win_width=4.0,
        low_e_cut_kev=5.0,
        flux_floor_counts=20.0,
        auto_center=True,
        search_tol_kev=2.0,
    )

    edge_step = np.asarray(r["edge_step"], dtype=float)   # (H,W) Delta-OD
    snr = np.asarray(r["snr"], dtype=float)               # (H,W)
    field_measurable = bool(r.get("measurable", False))
    edge_used = float(r.get("edge_kev_used", edge_kev))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 2: per-pixel measurability mask.
    # Combine the field-level flux gate with a per-pixel SNR threshold
    # (the helper's own recommendation: snr > ~3). Also require a
    # physically sensible POSITIVE step (absorption edge => OD jumps up).
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    snr_thresh = 3.0
    good = np.isfinite(edge_step) & np.isfinite(snr)
    measurable_px = good & (snr > snr_thresh) & (edge_step > 0.0)

    # If the whole field is flux-starved at the K-edge, the helper flags
    # measurable=False. In that case per-pixel K-edge thickness is NOT
    # defensible -> keep only pixels that individually survive a stricter
    # SNR gate, and if essentially none do, return an all-zero map
    # (honest "not measurable") rather than continuum-slope speckle.
    if not field_measurable:
        measurable_px = good & (snr > 5.0) & (edge_step > 0.0)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 3: light spatial de-speckling of the mask.
    # A real sputtered film is spatially contiguous; remove isolated
    # salt-and-pepper survivors by requiring local neighbour support.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    import scipy.ndimage as ndi
    mask_f = measurable_px.astype(float)
    # neighbour count (8-connectivity) via uniform smoothing
    neigh = ndi.uniform_filter(mask_f, size=3) * 9.0 - mask_f
    contiguous = measurable_px & (neigh >= 2.0)  # need >=2 measurable neighbours
    # keep original if de-speckling would erase everything real
    if contiguous.sum() >= 0.3 * measurable_px.sum() and measurable_px.sum() > 0:
        final_mask = contiguous
    else:
        final_mask = measurable_px

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 4: build the reported Au_Edge_Step map (Delta-OD).
    # Non-Au / low-flux / non-measurable pixels -> NaN so the spatial
    # map shows only the (candidate) sputtered-Au footprint cleanly.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    au_edge_step = np.where(final_mask, edge_step, np.nan)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 5: convert Delta-OD to Au thickness via the K-edge jump in
    # the mass-attenuation coefficient.
    #   delta(OD) = delta(mu/rho) * rho * t
    #   t = delta(OD) / (delta(mu/rho) * rho)
    # Get mu/rho just below and just above the K-edge from NIST tables.
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    rho_au = 19.32  # g/cm^3 bulk Au
    e_below = np.array([edge_used - 1.0])   # ~79.8 keV (below K-edge)
    e_above = np.array([edge_used + 0.8])   # ~81.6 keV (above K-edge)
    mu_below = float(attenuation('Au', e_below)[0])   # cm^2/g
    mu_above = float(attenuation('Au', e_above)[0])   # cm^2/g
    dmu = mu_above - mu_below                          # jump in mu/rho (cm^2/g)

    if dmu <= 0 or not np.isfinite(dmu):
        # guard: attenuation table should give a positive K-edge jump
        dmu = np.nan

    # thickness in cm, then convert to micrometers
    thickness_cm = au_edge_step / (dmu * rho_au)
    au_thickness_um = thickness_cm * 1.0e4  # cm -> um

    # physically thickness must be non-negative; clip tiny negatives to 0
    au_thickness_um = np.where(
        np.isfinite(au_thickness_um) & (au_thickness_um < 0.0),
        0.0, au_thickness_um
    )

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Diagnostics / sanity anchors
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    field_step = float(r.get("field_step", np.nan))
    coverage = float(np.mean(final_mask)) * 100.0

    maps = {
        "Au_Edge_Step": au_edge_step.astype(float),
        "Au_Thickness": au_thickness_um.astype(float),
        "Edge_SNR": np.where(final_mask, snr, np.nan).astype(float),
    }

    units = {
        "Au_Edge_Step": "optical depth (Delta -ln(I/I0))",
        "Au_Thickness": "um",
        "Edge_SNR": "a.u.",
    }

    description = (
        "Per-pixel Au K-edge (80.8 keV) analysis. Transmission spectra are "
        "formed as I/I0 against the same-grid baseline_I0 operand and worked "
        "in optical depth -ln(I/I0) by the measure_edge_step helper, which "
        "picks robust wide pre-/post-edge continuum windows, gates on photon "
        "flux, and reports per-pixel SNR + a field measurability flag "
        "(canceling smooth continuum by a differential across the edge rather "
        "than a global model). Au_Edge_Step is the K-edge OD jump, reported "
        "only where the edge is measurable (per-pixel SNR>3, positive step, "
        "spatial-contiguity de-speckle); non-Au/low-flux pixels are NaN. "
        "Au_Thickness inverts delta(OD)=delta(mu/rho)*rho*t using the NIST "
        "Au mass-attenuation jump across the K-edge (mu_above-mu_below = "
        f"{dmu:.4g} cm^2/g) and bulk density 19.32 g/cm^3, in micrometers. "
        "We deliberately stay on the Au-specific K-edge instead of pivoting "
        "to the non-specific L3 edge; if the K-edge is flux-starved the mask "
        "collapses to few/no pixels rather than fabricating continuum-slope "
        f"speckle. Field-mean K-edge step={field_step:.4g} OD, "
        f"edge_kev_used={edge_used:.3f}, coverage={coverage:.1f}%."
    )

    return {"maps": maps, "units": units, "description": description}

issues.problem: The Au K-edge at 80.8 keV lands where the source bremsstrahlung flux has nearly collapsed: the mean spectrum shows counts dropping from ~500 near 60 keV to essentially the noise floor (~10-20 counts) already by 80-90 keV, and virtually zero above ~120 keV. At 80.8 keV there are only a handful of photons per pixel, so any '-ln(I/I0) jump' there is dominated by Poisson noise, not a real absorption edge. The physical tells confirm this is NOT the Au K-edge signal: (1) the extracted 'edge_step' map is a smooth top-to-bottom gradient with a curved boundary—this is a beam/flux-profile or path-length artifact, not a sputtered-film morphology; (2) the recovered Delta-OD values are enormous (mean 0.92, up to 2.0), which via Delta(mu)*rho would imply hundreds of microns of gold—physically impossible for a sputtered layer (typically nm to sub-micron) and inconsistent with any K-edge jump measurable given the near-zero flux there. The apparent 'edge' is almost certainly the flux gate/continuum-window fit latching onto the steep bremsstrahlung roll-off and detector-response features (note the strong peaks at ~60 and ~67 keV, which are fluorescence/scatter lines, not Au K). Corrective direction: (a) verify there is genuine transmitted flux at 80.8 keV—gate far more aggressively (flux_floor well above 20 counts at the POST-edge window energy, not the field mean) and reject the whole field if post-edge counts are at the noise floor; (b) confirm the pre/post windows (76-80 keV vs 81.6-85 keV) actually straddle a step in -ln(I/I0) rather than fitting the monotonic bremsstrahlung decay—the current windows are almost certainly measuring source spectral shape; (c) sanity-check thickness against a physical bound (sputtered Au ≪ few microns) and against the sample being localized, not a full-field gradient. As reported, this captures a flux/beam-profile artifact, not the sputtered Au distribution.

The map does capture a coherent (non-trivial) spatial pattern, so it is not a pure-noise collapse — but the VALUE is physically indefensible and the morphology points to an artifact, not the Au distribution. (1) Magnitude: mean 74.5 um and max 166 um of gold. A 74 um Au layer corresponds to a K-edge OD jump of order ~1 (delta(mu/rho)~6.8 cm^2/g x rho 19.32 x 0.0074 cm ~ 0.95). A 'sputtered' Au layer is expected in the nm-to-~1 um range; the reported thickness is 2-3 orders of magnitude too large, which alone is a strong plausibility failure. (2) Independent cross-check: if the field truly averaged ~74 um Au, the FIELD-MEAN spectrum would show an obvious discontinuous drop (factor ~e in transmitted counts) at 80.8 keV. The provided mean spectrum shows no visible K-edge step there — only the fluorescence/scatter peaks near 60-70 keV and a smooth continuum decline through 80 keV. The absence of a mean-spectrum edge commensurate with the reported thickness indicates the per-pixel 'edge steps' are inflated. (3) Morphology: the result is a smooth top-to-bottom (curved) gradient that decays into a NaN region at the bottom — this is the classic signature of tracking detector FLUX/geometry (counts at 80.8 keV are only ~tens in the mean), where -ln(I/I0) is noisily amplified into spurious positive steps in the low-flux/high-attenuation region, rather than a sputtered film or coupon. Corrective direction: (a) verify that a real baseline_I0 was supplied (the code silently falls back to a field-median pseudo-I0, which corrupts absolute OD); (b) tighten measure_edge_step's flux gate (raise flux_floor_counts well above ~20 and raise the SNR threshold) at these high energies where counts collapse, and confirm the retained pixels actually show the 80.8 keV step against the mean spectrum; (c) if after proper flux gating the edge is not measurable over the field, report non-measurable instead of a flux-driven gradient.

The result must be rejected on a SIGNAL/SOUNDNESS flaw that the code's own flux gate should have caught but did not: the mean spectrum shows transmitted flux collapsing to the noise floor (~10-30 counts, and essentially ~0 by 100 keV) well before the Au K-edge at 80.8 keV. Reading the mean spectrum at 80-85 keV, the field-mean counts are in the low tens at best, so the post-edge continuum window (81.6-85 keV) has almost no genuine transmitted photons to define an -ln(I/I0) step. This is exactly the failure mode flagged in Attempt 1 (bremsstrahlung flux collapse at/above the edge), and the two attempts converge on the SAME physical fact — not on the same measured magnitude of a real edge. The reported Delta-OD map (mean 0.024, positive, dome-shaped, salt-and-pepper coverage at 24%) is the signature of Poisson/continuum-slope noise being rectified into a positive 'jump' by the (edge_step > 0) mask, NOT a real absorption edge: a genuine sputtered-Au film would give a spatially coherent, contiguous edge-step region, whereas here the finite pixels are scattered speckle with a dome outline that mirrors the source flux/beam profile rather than a deposited coupon. The core problem is that FLUX_FLOOR=60 counts was evidently satisfied by the field-median over the window, but the median is dominated by low-energy channels leaking into the flux check; the true post-edge (81-85 keV) flux is far below any level that supports a 0.2 keV-resolution K-edge measurement. Corrective direction: (1) evaluate the flux gate strictly on the actual post-edge window counts (81.6-85 keV) per pixel, not a field-median that can be inflated by out-of-window channels, and raise the effective requirement so that pixels with only tens of post-edge counts are rejected; (2) require the edge-step region to be spatially contiguous (connected-component / morphological filter), rejecting isolated single-pixel 'positive' steps that are the fingerprint of rectified noise; (3) confirm with a hard cross-check that the mean spectrum shows a resolvable step at 80.8 keV before trusting any per-pixel map. As reported, this is a flux-starved edge that should have returned the non-measurable NaN maps.

The method's own flux-sanity logic is the correct physics, but the result contradicts it: the mean spectrum shows counts collapsing from ~500 near 60 keV to essentially the noise floor by 75-85 keV (well below ~50 counts at 80.8 keV, and continuing down toward ~10 counts). This is exactly the flux-starved regime the code was written to reject (FLUX_FLOOR=60). The fact that measure_edge_step returned 'measurable' and 1544 pixels passed SNR>=3 means the post-edge window flux gate was satisfied on numbers that the field-mean spectrum shows are at/near the noise floor — the SNR is being computed on Poisson fluctuations of a near-zero continuum, not a real absorption edge. Corroborating evidence: (1) Attempt 1 already produced a 'coherent spatial pattern' with 'physically indefensible' values from this same edge and was rejected as an artifact; (2) the current thickness histogram is a broad ~1-3 um distribution capped hard at the 5 um MAX_PHYS_UM bound, with mean 1.88 um — sputtered Au is typically tens to hundreds of nm, and a smooth noise-driven distribution pressed against an imposed clip bound is the signature of an artifact, not a real thickness map; (3) the map morphology (salt-and-pepper speckle with a rounded top edge tracking the flux/beam envelope, not a coherent film) points to beam/flux geometry, not Au localization. Corrective direction: this K-edge is not measurable with a 160 kVp bremsstrahlung source whose flux dies before 80.8 keV — do not report thickness from the K-edge. Instead locate/quantify Au via its L-edges (~11.9/13.7/14.4 keV) or the Au fluorescence/L-lines that fall in the high-flux 10-60 keV region visible in the spectrum, where photon statistics actually support an edge/line measurement. If the K-edge must be used, the flux gate must be evaluated on the actual per-pixel post-edge counts (which here are ~10-20, below the 60 floor), which would correctly return the non-measurable branch.

The method pivoted from the Au K-edge (80.8 keV) to the Au L3 edge (~11.9 keV), but the evidence shows this L3-edge result is an artifact, not a genuine Au signal. SIGNAL/MORPHOLOGY problem: the Au_Edge_Step map does NOT show a coherent sputtered-film footprint — it is a diffuse salt-and-pepper scatter across the lower field plus a bright RIM/EDGE concentration along the top and left/right borders (the classic vignetting/edge artifact signature). A real sputtered Au coupon would produce a spatially contiguous region; this map has no such connected structure and the strongest steps sit precisely on the frame border, which is a hallmark of continuum/vignetting leakage rather than a real edge jump.
